title: The four types of data scale
body:
- Nominal data are categories with no ranking. You can count frequencies and find the most common category, but can't calculate averages or measure distances between categories.
- Ordinal data have ranked categories but unequal gaps. You can identify the median and compare relative positions, but the differences between values are not universally defined and comparable.
- Interval data have equal spacing but no true "absolute" zero - temperature scales or survey scores using standardized scales. The difference between any two values are measurable and comparable.
- Ratio data have equal spacing and a true "absolute" zero point. This zero indicates None of what's measured by the variable.
common_mistake: Students swap the pairs — saying nominal and ordinal are quantitative while interval and ratio are categorical. All four are scales; nominal and ordinal are the categorical pair.

title: Choosing the best measure of central tendency
body:
The "best" measure of central tendency depends on your business context and data characteristics.
- Use the median when dealing with skewed data like salaries, customer spending, or deal sizes where outliers would distort the picture. It shows what most of your business actually experiences.
- Use the mean (average) when you need to understand total impact or when data is normally distributed. It's essential for financial planning, resource allocation, and forecasting since it accounts for every data point.
- Use the mode when identifying the most common category or value, such as the most popular product feature, frequent customer complaint, or typical order size.

title: Interpreting the mean of one variable
body: The mean can be interpreted as the "typical" value in a given context (context involves what is the variable and unit of measure).

title: Interpreting the median of a variable
body:
The median represents the middle value when your data is arranged from lowest to highest - it's the point where 50% of observations fall below and 50% fall above.

The median reveals the "typical" experience of your customers, employees, or business units. Unlike the average, it isn't skewed by extreme outliers, making it particularly valuable for real-world business conditions where data might be heavily skewed.

title: Interpreting a Pareto bar chart
body:
A Pareto chart reveals which factors drive the majority of your business problems or outcomes, helping you prioritize where to focus limited resources for maximum impact. Typically, a small number of categories (around 20%) account for the large majority (around 80%) of the total effect.

Note: given the nominal variable, the 80/20 insight may only partially apply or not at all apply.
common_mistake: The 80/20 split is treated as a rule. With few categories, or a 60/40 split, it may only partly apply or not at all.

title: Interpreting skewness
body:
Technically: Skewness measures the asymmetry of data distribution - whether values cluster more toward one end of the range, creating a "tail" on the opposite side. Understanding skewness helps choose appropriate benchmarks and realistic targets, since heavily skewed data makes the mean misleading for typical performance expectations.

Business Insights: When interpreting, we focus on two perspectives,
- where most data are centered on
- there are "more than expected" (not most) of observations in the skewed side of data.
managerial_phrasing: Say where most of the data sits, then "more than expected" values in the skewed tail.
common_mistake: Skewness is asked about for two categorical variables. It only describes a quantitative distribution's shape.

title: Interpreting standard deviation
body:
Technically: standard means Average, and deviation means the difference between actual data and the typical value (the mean).

Insights: based on empirical rule, about 2/3 or 68% of the observations are within one stdev around the mean. This indicates the most typical range of values.
managerial_phrasing: Frame as the typical range: about 2/3 of observations sit within one stdev of the mean.

title: Using a z-value to judge how extreme a data point is
body:
Z-value measures how many standard deviations a data point is away from the mean. It standardizes different variables onto the same scale for comparison.

Insights: Z-values help identify outliers and benchmark performance across different metrics.
- |z| > 3 means the data is very unlikely or uncommon
- 2 < |z| < 3 means the data is unlikely or uncommon
- 1 < |z| < 2 means the data is likely or common
- |z| < 1 means the data is very common.
managerial_phrasing: Report as very common (|z|<1), common (1-2), uncommon (2-3), very uncommon (>3).

title: Developing the null hypothesis
body:
Null hypothesis is what we expect things to happen when there is no difference, no effect, no change. The key here is to translate the concept of "nothing" in given context.

Ex: in the context of marketing promotion, "nothing" means the promotion has no impact (on the revenue).
managerial_phrasing: Translate "nothing happens" into the business context before writing Ho.

title: Interpreting a p-value
body: p-value is a special significance for testing slope in regressions. The null hypothesis here is there is no relationship or slope equals to 0. p-value can be compared to 5% the same way as any other significance.
common_mistake: Evaluating the significance of a slope is confused with interpreting the slope. The p-value says whether there is a relationship; the slope says how much.

title: Understanding significance
body: Significance describes how likely a sample can be observed given the null hypothesis of the population. The smaller is the significance, the more unlikely to observe our sample, which means the sample is more significantly indicating the true population is different from the expectation based on the null hypothesis.

title: Interpreting the slope of a simple regression
body: In simple regression, slope can be interpreted as how much does Y change per unit of X, on average. We can then combine this general format with corresponding context. If the X variable is categorical, we need to focus on the comparison between categories.

title: Interpreting R-squared
body: R2 tells us how much the X variable can explain the variations in the Y variable. Note it's the variation of Y, not Y itself. And the variation is measured against the corresponding mean.

title: Interpreting a coefficient in a multiple regression
body: The interpretation of regression coefficient in multiple regression is similar to that in simple regression, ex how much does Y change per unit of X, on average. However, due to the existence of other variables in the model, we need to add an additional phrase, such as controlling for other variables in the model.
managerial_phrasing: Add "controlling for the other variables in the model" to the per-unit statement.

title: What collinearity and multicollinearity are
body:
Collinearity occurs when the X variables in a model are also correlated with each other. As such the impact of each of the variables are confounded, and simple regression is not enough to differentiate the direct effect of a variable from the indirect effect.

Ex: the size and number of bedrooms of a house is highly correlated. The impact of size on house price can be directly due to larger size and/or due to more bedrooms.

title: What collinearity does to your coefficients
body:
Depending on the degree of collinearity, the regression coefficients in simple and multiple regressions are different.
- If the direct and indirect effects are in the same direction, the multiple regression coefficients will be weaker than that in simple regression. Ex: when using both sqft and bedrooms to predict price.
- If the direct and indirect effects are in different direction, the multiple regression coefficients will be stronger than that in simple regression. Ex: when using both bedrooms and age to predict price.
Note that stronger or weaker is referring to the size of the coefficient, not the sign.
common_mistake: Students expect the coefficient to get stronger when the direct and indirect effects point the same way. It gets weaker; stronger happens when they point in opposite directions.

title: Do I remove all insignificant categories of a categorical variable
body: When building a model, we should evaluate each variable that is not significant carefully. If the variable is quantitative or binary, then yes, it should excluded. If the variable is a dummy variable that belongs to a categorical variable with more than 2 categories, then we need to evaluate the  categorical variable as a whole, not just the category itself.

title: What is backwards deduction process
body: It is a model building process that starts with a regression with all the appropriate X variables, and then removes the worst variable one at a time until all the remaining variables are significant.
